Vox Vox by Thomas Organ browse by type distortion/fuzz/overdrive fuzz browse by enclosure pedal Vox (by Jen) V828 Tone Bender Published on October 25, 2008 Vox by Jen Vox by Thomas Organ fuzz pedal Information an old Vox catalog A foot operated distortion accessory. Electronically controlled fuzzy distortion effects are produced with a foot tap. The Vox Tone Bender creates harmonics that are nonexistent in the fundamental signal. Gives the exciting sounds of many of the world's foremost Rock'n'Roll groups. The Vox V828 Tone Bender is a germanium fuzz pedal produced in Italy by Jen for Vox and distributed by Thomas Organ in the United States during the late 1960s and early 1970s. It is one of the most recognizable versions of the Tone Bender family and became associated with the classic British fuzz sound of the era. The V828 circuit is closely related to the Sola Sound Tone Bender Mk1.5 and the Dallas Arbiter Fuzz Face. It uses two germanium transistors, most often the Italian made SFT363 and SFT337, to create a thick, sustaining fuzz with smooth overdrive characteristics. Compared to the later V8281, the V828 generally provides more low end and a fuller, creamier tone. The pedal features two chicken head knobs for simple control. The Attack knob adjusts the amount of fuzz saturation and sustain, while the Level knob sets the overall output. Like other germanium fuzz designs, the V828 interacts dynamically with a guitar's volume control, allowing the sound to clean up when rolling back the input signal. Controls Attack: adjusts fuzz intensity and sustain Level: sets output volume Connections 1 x 1/4" input 1 x 1/4" output Powered by 9V battery Technical Specifications Circuit type: two transistor germanium fuzz inspired by Tone Bender Mk1.5 Transistors: typically SFT363 and SFT337 germanium Capacitors: period correct Ducati and Mullard components Potentiometers: 50kΩ Level pot, Attack pot with bypass capacitor around 15 µF Resistors: carbon composition, includes 1kΩ between transistor collector resistors to boost treble and output Grounding: positive ground PNP design Enclosure: die cast aluminum case in black crinkle or grey hammerite finish Highlights Italian built Vox fuzz distributed by Thomas Organ in the US Delivers thick, creamy fuzz with long sustain

Even though the Gibson Maestro Fuzz Tone featured in the Rolling Stones 1965 hit (I Can't Get No) Satisfaction had been introduced in 1962, the effect pedal had previously gained little traction in the marketplace. The chart success of "Satisfaction" convinced every guitarist that they needed a fuzz tone. Various manufacturers in the US and UK tooled up to produce them. Gary Hurst, a UK based amplifier tech, started to produce and market fuzz tones in 1965. One of his early accounts was the Musical Exchange in London. Hurst soon teamed with the Musical Exchange to produce pedals under the Sola Sound brand. Anxious to enter the fuzz tone market, JMI entered into an agreement with the Musical Exchange to purchase Sola Sound fuzz pedals rebranded with the Vox "Tone Bender" name. A 1968 purchase order from JMI to the Musical Exchange for Tone Benders can be seen below. Thomas Organ, the American distributor of Vox, chose to bypass Sola Sound. Thomas Organ had a close relationship with the Italian manufacturer JEN. The V828 Vox Tone Bender and many Vox organs for the US market were produced by JEN. The two pedals shown on the top of this page are examples of the Thomas V828 Tone Bender produced by JEN. Some of these pedals were finished in black "crinkle coat" paint while others were adorned with gray hammertone. The Sola Sound Tone Bender had a sand cast aluminum case. The JEN case was die cast aluminum. A steel base covered the bottom of the pedal. The pedal was powered by a 9V battery clipped to the inside bottom of the base. The Tone Bender circuit was similar to the input stage of the Vox T.60 amplifier head. The JEN Tone Bender circuit included an SFT363 and an SFT337 germanium transistor, two capacitors and six resistors. The Sola Tone Bender circuit was similar but substituted a pair of OC76 germanium transistors for the SFT363 and SFT337. One rotary control adjusted output level, a second adjusted the "attack" or intensity of the fuzz.
